column3: A name only it gave is a guess: no source asserted it.

Without `-live` nothing is looked up, so such a name is printed as a candidate with `"unverified": true` in `-json`: no source asserted it and nothing confirmed it, and it is among the `raw candidates` like every other name.
`-guesses=false` holds them back instead: they are not printed, counted as `guesses held back`, and a note says how many.

Without `-live` subdomain.center is asked once, as subfinder asks it.
With `-live` every guess of a sample is looked up at `-dns-rate`, as `subfinder | dnsx` looks up every name it is given: your rate is the bound on the cost.
A zone is probed for a wildcard only when a guess in it resolves, once, with one query when it answers NXDOMAIN.
The first sample is always checked in full, at any rate: it is what `subfinder | dnsx` checks.

A further sample is taken while the last had a new name that resolves, or while the names seen are under 95% of the pool that the samples' repeats estimate (Schnabel's estimate, which needs one repeat: so the second sample is always taken), up to 12, and only if it fits the 20 s left of the budget for further samples.
The budget starts when the first sample has been checked, and a sample is expected to cost what the last one did, so at a polite `-dns-rate` the first sample can be all there is time for.
`-guess-samples N` goes further: up to N samples while each finds a new name that resolves or the pool is not yet covered, with no time budget, and N may be above 12.
`-guess-samples 1` takes the first only. Without `-live` nothing resolves, so the samples go on only while the pool is not yet covered.
A note names a stop that was a bound, says how many samples were left untaken and names the flag
Names that could not be checked (the resolvers failed, or the run ended first) are counted as `not checked` and left out; `azhaq resume` checks them.
A source that answers a 5xx (a 500, 502, 503 or 504, such as subdomain.center's `503 {"error": "server busy (64 queries in flight)"}`) is asked again the same way
When a source still fails, its reason carries the status and the first words of the server's body
A 501 or 505 is not asked again.
One that asks for longer, or keeps refusing, is not waited for.
A name that only `-w` or `-permute` guessed, and a CNAME target, is not stored: those can be asked again, and the history is the memory of what passive sources answered.
At most 200,000 names are kept per domain. The ones unseen the longest go first.
With `-live`, a stored name counts only if it resolves now, and not to a wildcard.
Stale names drop out (one only a wildcard answers is counted in `wildcard answers left out`), and a name a source missed this time comes back.
Without `-live` no DNS lookup is made.
The names are stored only once a source gave them or DNS confirmed them, so they are not guesses.

A stored name that a source gave again is not flagged: its `source` is that source, and `history` comes last in `sources`. Every name a source gave and a run kept is stored, so flagging them all would flag nearly every name after the first run.
It gives the path, the names the file gave the run (before any check) and the names the run wrote (a name no lookup checked is not written). For more than three domains one note counts them all.

Without `-db` there is nothing to resume, and the note says to run again with `-db FILE`, or without `-live` to list them unverified.
A name is in one of three tiers, and the tiers are never mixed:
Without `-live` every printed row is a `candidate`, and the summary says `DNS-confirmed not asked (-live)`: nothing is confirmed, whatever the sources think of it.
The summary says `HTTP-confirmed not asked (-http)` without it.

The raw candidates that did not resolve are not printed: they are in `raw candidates` and `did not resolve`, so the two counts show how many names the sources gave and how many of them exist in DNS. `raw candidates` less `did not resolve` is `resolved from sources`, which `DNS-confirmed` includes along with the names found by guessing and as CNAME targets.

A `tiers:` note states the counts: `tiers: 526 raw candidates (what the sources gave; a row's sources say who); 6 DNS-confirmed (resolved); HTTP-confirmed not asked (-http): a candidate is never counted as confirmed`.

The estimate is made for each tier and labelled with it (`coverage (raw candidates)`, `coverage (DNS-confirmed)`): a tier's note counts only the names that reached it, so a confirmed tier's pool is the confirmed names the independent sources know. It is a Chao1 estimate over how many independent sources gave each name: S + f1²/(2·f2). Here f1 is the number of names given by one source, and f2 the number given by two. With f2 = 0 it is S + f1(f1−1)/2.
Independent means every source except the ones that pad their answer (subdomain.center) and `history`. A name only those gave is in the output but not in the count.
The raw candidate tier counts every name the sources gave.

It estimates what the sources know, not every name that exists, and the note says so first. It prints no percentage: 1400 of 1609 is a share of what the sources hold, not of the subdomains the domain has.

With `-live` the names of the DNS-confirmed tier that the pool does not hold (the name history, guesses DNS confirmed, CNAME targets) are counted apart from it, and the two add up to the names printed.
`-recursive` runs only the sources that handle subdomains of subdomains.

A value you give also caps the names `-w` and `-permute` ask, together, first the words and then the variations: the guesses past it are not asked, so `asked by guessing` is at most the cap, the run exits 4, `stopped` names `-max-names`, and a note says how many guesses it held back. Without it, a guess list has no cap: the cap's default is for the names looked up, never for a wordlist.
An HTTP proxy cannot, so crt.sh is then asked in the JSON API only, and a note says so.
A source that needs a key and has none is not run.
Without a key it is asked again while its last round gave a name that resolves and no other source had, or while the names seen are not yet most of its pool: see [Guesses](#guesses).

`-max-time` bounds the whole run, this source's rounds and the lookups of its guesses too: when it passes, the names gathered are kept, the ones whose lookup was cut are counted as `not checked`, and its row says the run's time limit cut it short. `-source-timeout` bounds each of its calls and, with them, half the time it spends asking; the lookups of its guesses are paced by `-dns-rate`, not by `-source-timeout`.

`-max-time` is the whole run's wall-clock bound, as `-timeout` is, and the shorter of the two applies: the sources, subdomain.center's rounds, and the DNS checks of `-live`, `-w` and `-permute` all end with it. The run exits 4, `stopped` names `-max-time`, a note counts the names not asked in DNS, and `azhaq resume` asks them.

column3: A generated name (a guess of subdomain.center, `-w`, `-permute`, a name only the history held) is asked up to 2 times, as dnsx's `-retry` default: made-up names mostly do not exist, and each attempt of a name no resolver answers is a paced query, so a third is 50% more time on a zone whose servers are silent.
`azhaq dns -retry N` sets the attempts for every name, generated ones too.
Resolvers that fail take turns: each is asked in its turn, so `-dns-rate` is the pace of each, not of one.
Without `-dns-rate` a late attempt is also hedged: another is sent beside it and the first answer wins.
With `-dns-rate` nothing is hedged, because a hedge spends a slot of your rate on every answer that is merely slow: a zone that answers in 1.2 s costs one query a guess.

A name that no resolver answered in its attempts is asked again in a second pass at a quarter of the concurrency. When none of a batch of 16 names or more was answered, the resolvers are down, not busy, and there is no second pass.

The second pass asks 16 of those names first, spread over the list and once each, and ends there when none of them is answered: the zone's servers are not answering, the rest would fail alike at the cost of every attempt again, and they keep the first failure (`no answer`, or `not checked` for a guess). When one is answered, every name still failed is asked in full.

crt.sh's database is asked for a quarter of `-source-timeout` and then left, whether or not the driver gives up: a connection that hangs holds the source for the quarter, not for the whole timeout, and the JSON API gets the rest.
A name is live when DNS has a record for it: an address, directly or through its CNAME chain, or a CNAME whose chain ends without one (marked `cname_only`).
`true` on a name whose addresses are all loopback, private (RFC 1918, `fc00::/7`) or link-local: it resolves, but not to an address the internet reaches.
Without `-live` nothing is looked up. The guesses are listed with `"unverified": true`, and the summary counts them.

With `-live`, a guess that could not be checked, near `-timeout` or `-max-time` or with the DNS lookups failing, is left out and counted as `not checked`. The source's status says `N of its names not checked`, and `azhaq resume` checks them.

Resolves names for any record type and leaves out wildcard answers.
Leaves out a name that only resolves through a wildcard zone.
`dns` neither reads nor writes the name history `subs` keeps under `azhaq-data/` (or the directory you name)
`dns` sends DNS queries and nothing else.
When a line is a record (`-resp`, `-resp-only`, a transfer), it counts both: `13 records of 12 names`.

`requests` is 0 for `dns`: its questions go to resolvers, not targets. `dns_queries` counts them (the retries and the wildcard probes too, so it is more than `asked`), and equals the ledger's `DNS queries` line count, with or without `-ledger`.

Text and `-json` both give a row only to a name that has a record of the types asked. A is the type when no flag names one, as in dnsx. A name that does not exist, or has no such record, such as a TXT-only name when A is asked, gets no row and is counted as `did not resolve`. So `asked` minus `did not resolve` is the number of rows.

With `-rcode`, only the names whose answer has that code get a row, with its `status_code`. That is how to list the names that do not exist. A name whose CNAME points at what is gone is not one of them: its own code is `NOERROR`, and the target's `NXDOMAIN` is its `cname_status`.
With `-all`, `-any` or `-axfr`, `-json` gives a row to every name a resolver answered, including one with no record at all.

With `-response-type-filter` and no type flag, `-json` gives a row to every answered name that has none of the records filtered, as dnsx does: `-rtf a` keeps the names that have only AAAA, TXT, MX or SRV, that have no record (NODATA), that do not exist, and the CNAME-only ones, and leaves out the names with an A. In text, a kept name prints the records it has, so one with none prints nothing.
with `takeover`, whichever types are asked, unless `-no-takeover` is given
`-all` asks A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, SOA, TXT, SRV and CAA of a name: not PTR (`-ptr`) and not ANY (`-any`). AXFR is asked with `-axfr` only, because it connects to the name servers.
An address gets PTR only.

With `-allow`, `-scope` or `-deny` given, a name server is asked only at an address the scope allows: its name being in the scope does not vouch for where it points. A name server whose address is outside is not contacted.
Without any scope flag, the name given is the scope, as before.

`left out` counts inputs that were not asked about:
an address or range without `-ptr`

A route whose GET answered 405, 400, 415 or 422 counts in full: the server has it, it only refused this request.
A row of such a route (`hint` coverage, status 404 or 410) is not an answer to anything:
Its path words and an exposed-file name weigh nothing, and its reasons say `unconfirmed: named by a script, not confirmed: GET 404`, not `answers 404`.

It still keeps the signals the script gives it (the fields it sends, a write without credentials), and it comes after every row the server confirmed (200, 401, 403, 405 and other 4xx that are not 404 or 410, 5xx), whatever their scores.
When nothing else is known of the route the row is left out.
An input name that most pages of an origin carry belongs to the site's template, such as a search box or a sign-in form in every page's header.
A script that names a route says the client calls it, not that the server has it, and a GET that answers 404 or 410 shows nothing of a POST-only route either.

the body showing SQL error text, a framework's debug page or a stack trace makes the row a finding
A served file whose bytes were not judged (a workspace made before the answers were kept) is a lead.
A bare 403 says only `forbidden` and weighs less (5, against 15): nothing in it shows that a session would change the answer.
Accounts for every target: it ends as a row, a failure (a row with `failed: true`) or a skip (named under `skipped` in the summary, with no row).
Sends other methods or your own request only when you ask: `-x` adds methods, `-request` sends a request file.
Always present on an answered row (a failed row has `input`, `host`, `url`, `port`, `scheme`, `timestamp`, `failed` and `error`):

The summary counts the rows that got an answer under `answered` and the ones that got none under `without an answer`, so the counts partition the rows, and says how many rows the matchers and filters left out.
A host that answered on no web port is a note, not a count: its rows are among those without an answer.
For a bare host it is httpx's form, the front page without a slash (`http://h`).
is answered with its status, headers and the first part of its body (up to 64 KiB, or what comes in 2 seconds), and then closed, not held until the timeout.
A target that got no answer, such as a name that does not resolve or a closed port, is a row with `failed: true` and an `error`.
The summary counts it under `without an answer`.

A plain request that is answered 400, or not answered (refused, closed, timed out, or a service that does not speak HTTP), is asked again over TLS, as httpx does. The 400 stays when TLS does not answer. A TLS request that is not answered is asked again over plain HTTP. Any other answer stands and the other scheme is not asked.
Every target given ends as a row, a failure or a skip.
It is never one answer and a `no answer` for the others.
Without `-p`, a URL or `host:port` is asked once, on its own port.
A bare name that has no address is a failed row for each port of `-p`, and `failures` counts each of them.

One slash goes between the two paths, a path that already ends with the other, or starts with it, is not repeated, the URL's query is kept and the path's own query is added to it, and the fragment is never sent.
Its favicon, redirects and second scheme do not.
`-rate N` paces every request instead.
azhaq never downloads the model. Without it, the command is a usage error, exit 2, that says where to fetch it: `the page classifier's model is not at …`.

A name whose only evidence is `size`, `lines` or `body` is checked once more before it is kept: four names no page reads, as long as it, are asked, and each answer it gave must differ from them and from the reference by more than the page shows by itself.
A name the page ignores (`utm_source`) is not reported. On a page that prints what it is sent, only the rename is judged.

When the page refuses a request without its input (400 or 422), asks the names not found again with the names found so far in every request, against a new reference taken the same way, and repeats while a pass finds more (at most 3 passes). A page that reports its required fields one at a time says nothing about the second until the first is given. A page that answers without input is not asked again.
`params -json` prints only these fields.
The run exits 3 when every page failed, and 0 when others gave their names (`-strict-exit` makes it 3).

A page not searched has a note that says why: it changes by itself, is not text, or is past `-params-per-host`. A page a `-deny-path` rule matches is listed under `skipped` with the rule, and nothing is sent to it. In `run -params`, a page that answered the run's own request as the origin answers a path that cannot exist, or with 401, 403 or 405, is not searched either (`-params-all` searches it); `azhaq params` asks the pages you give it all.
A page that answers names it does not read is listed in the summary's `notes`: see Details.

A page the request budget (`-max-requests`) ends is not lost: its row has the names established so far, the summary's `notes` say how many of the names were judged (`the request budget ended the search with 4 of 8 names judged (1 found so far)`), and the exit is 4.
A page answers names it does not read when most names of a group, or nearly every name tried alone, change its answer.
Names are sent in the order given, without duplicates. Every name is sent, with a session or without one.
A page that `-deny-path REGEX` matches is not searched, and the summary lists it under `skipped` with the rule.
A page that rate-limits (429, 418, 503) fails. The failure is listed as `failed` and retryable, with a note, and counted in `failures`.
A page that leaves requests unanswered fails too: listed as `failed`, not as retryable, with a note, and counted in `failures`.
Library scripts are not read for routes.

Every URL they give is requested, a GET operation of an API description (one that needs no path parameter and no required query parameter) and a GET form included, except one whose own path or API operation declares a state change
Asks only what a crawler does. The built-in path checks of `run` are off unless you add `-builtin-paths`.
`-sweep` means what it means on `run`: the IPv4 ranges and addresses `-allow` and `-scope` hold are start URLs too.
A note says that the built-in paths are `-builtin-paths` when `-sweep` is given without it.
`-kf all`, `-kf robotstxt` or `-kf sitemapxml` asks each web service only for its `robots.txt` and sitemaps and reads every entry.
Tells the page every unknown path gets from a real page with one request for a path that does not exist at the root and in each top-level directory (`/api/`, `/rest/`), not in every directory
`-builtin-paths` asks every directory, as `run` does (up to 24 per origin).
katana asks none.
column4: note:a statement about another tool, katana

column3: Lists the URLs it requested, each distinct URL once: every page, script and stylesheet it asked, less those that answered 404 or 410 and those that answered as the control does

A URL a page holds that the crawl did not request (past `-d`, a limit, a `-deny-path` rule, or a library script, an image or a font no step fetches) is listed too, marked `linked`, and the summary says how many.
Keeps apart what no page holds: routes that scripts call with POST, PUT or another method, routes with a parameter, views and sockets, and strings that scripts only name.
Never drops links without a word: the summary says how many it folded, left out of the list, kept out of the URLs or found outside the scope.
When a limit stops the crawl, it exits 4 and `azhaq resume` continues it.
The URLs that answered 404 or 410 or as the control does are [folded](#folded-rows) into the summary; `-all-rows` prints them.
Every row has a class, and `-json` prints it as `class`:
A `linked` row is a URL a page holds, as katana lists it, but the crawl did not ask it: it may answer 404, and the row says so by its class.

The summary's `counts` has `observed routes`, `linked routes`, `hint routes` and `named strings`, which add up to every URL row, and a note says exactly how many of the listed URLs are `linked` (`-silent` prints it on stderr too).
A page that holds hundreds of script strings does not bury the URLs the crawl saw: those strings are `named` and wait for `-hints`.
The images, fonts and media an explicit `-assets`, `-ndef` or `-em` asks for are listed as `linked` rows, requested or not.

counts the rows by class, `observed routes`, `linked routes`, `hint routes` and `named strings`, says how many listed URLs are `linked` (links or loads a page holds that the crawl did not request), and how many hints and named URLs were left out of the list (`-hints` lists them);
with `-hints`, counts both kinds of listed URL, and says where to look: routes that scripts call with other methods, and strings that scripts only name;
says how many POST forms `-submit-forms` sent, and which POST forms it did not send and why.

A crawl never drops links without a word: the summary says what became of them (`-silent` prints the notes on the list, and not the ones on rejected strings and on links outside the scope). When `-max-items`, `-max-requests`, `-mdp` or the run's `-timeout` stops it, the run exits 4 and `azhaq resume` continues it.
One URL per line: every page and script the crawl asked and whose answer is its own, and every URL a page links or loads that it did not, each distinct URL once.
The folded rows are left out ([Folded rows](#folded-rows)); `-all-rows` lists them. The routes only scripts and descriptions name, and the hints, are left out unless `-hints` is given.

The summary says how many URLs it listed that the crawl never requested, and how many hints and named URLs it left out (with `-silent` too: one line each on stderr, `N listed URLs are links or loads a page holds that the crawl did not request …` and `N hints and M named URLs were left out of the list`, and in the `-json` summary's notes).

A route a script names, `/catalog?category=Gin` in an object on `/catalog`, is a line when the crawl asked for it: at `-d 2` it is requested, so it is `observed`; past the depth it is not requested, so it is `named` and `-hints` lists it.

A link is a line either way: at `-d 1` the links of the pages at depth 1 are not requested, katana prints them with `"error":"max depth reached"` and no response, and azhaq lists them as `linked` rows.
column4: test:cmd/azhaq:TestCrawlListsWhatPagesLink,TestCrawlJSONLLineOfAURLNotAskedHasNoResponse;note:what katana prints is a statement about another tool

column3: `-per-template N` limits how many URLs of one template (`/item?id={n}`) are asked, not how many are listed. `crawl` and `run` ask every one by default, as katana does, and neither caps the tasks a run starts unless `-max-items` says so.
Every script a page loads or a script imports is listed once the crawl has requested it, when it is in the crawl's scope.

A library script (`jquery-3.2.1.min.js`, `bootstrap.min.js`, which azhaq does not read for routes) and an image or font a page loads are requested by no crawl step, so the library is a `linked` row in the default list; images, fonts and media are on katana's default extension list and wait for `-assets`.
The extension list leaves out only the images, fonts and media of it (`-assets` lists them): the `.pdf` and `.txt` URLs are rows.
`run`'s map lists every row, scripts and images included.
Views (`client-route`) and sockets (`websocket`) are `hint` rows, listed with `-json -hints` only, as routes with a parameter are.

The summary counts the others in a line of their class each, with what each class was measured against, and `-all-rows` lists every row as katana does (`-json` lists every row, a folded one marked `fold`):

`catchall`: URLs whose answer is the control's own page, equal byte for byte once the requested path is taken out of both (a page that only has its shape, such as an item page that prints its own number, stays listed), the request for a path that cannot exist at the root or in a top-level directory.
`not-found`: URLs the crawl requested and the server answered 404 or 410, with their templates (`/api/Feedbacks/{n} ×12`).
A URL a script or a description names stays out of the list unless `-hints` lists it, and is not folded then.

The counts `folded catchall`, `folded not-found` and `folded beyond-depth` are the rows each class left out of the list; the rest of `counts` is of the rows printed, and the summary's `folds` says the same as `-json`'s. `-no-catchall` leaves the catch-all rows out of every view.
A crawl's rows are not all URLs that were requested, so the number of rows is no number to set beside katana's.
column4: test:cmd/azhaq:TestCrawlSummaryCountsEachKindOfRow;note:advice about comparing with another tool, katana

column3: `requested`, `not requested` and `templates` add up to every URL row. So do the four class counts. The rows printed and the rows left out add up to them too, and a crawl whose counts do not add up to its rows ends with exit 1 and an internal error instead of a complete summary.

`-json -hints` prints every row the extension list and the filters did not leave out, templates included, and `-rejected` adds the rejected strings as lines of their own, which the number of results counts.
The note says how many were not requested.
`-silent -hints` adds the routes only scripts name, which katana's `-jsl` lists too.
column4: test:cmd/azhaq:TestCrawlListsAScriptsRouteOnlyWhenItWasAsked;note:what katana's -jsl lists is a statement about another tool

column3: These filters limit what is printed, not what is crawled.
`-em php,html` lists only those extensions. `none` stands for URLs without one.
Every form is a `forms` entry of its page: `method`, `action`, `enctype`, `fields`, `files`.
A GET form can delete or log out: it is asked like any link, and `-deny-path` keeps its action out.
`-no-form-fill` does not fill GET forms.
A POST form is sent only with `-submit-forms`, with the same values, urlencoded.
A POST form is not sent when it uploads a file (`multipart`), has nothing to send, posts outside the crawl's scope, or its address matches a `-deny-path` rule. Its name decides nothing.
A form whose action is empty or `#` submits to its own page: its `action` is the page's URL, and it is handled like any other.
The summary says how many POST forms were sent, and names each one that was not and why, such as `a POST form to /upload was not submitted: it uploads a file or has nothing to send`.
They are not pages. A GET may answer 404 or 405.
A string that a script only names, with no call, is a `named` row when a GET fails. Its `proof` is `GET answers 404; found only in scripts, method unknown`.
Library scripts are not read for routes: `react`, `jquery` and `angular`, also under a versioned name such as `angular_1-7-7.js`.
A URL that was found and not asked has no `response`.
`-rejected` lists the strings read from scripts and pages and kept out of the URLs. They are never asked.
a route a script's client asks under its declared base, and a key of a module map or a case label
`-do` lists the URLs found outside the crawl's scope. They are never asked.

With no `-allow` and no `-scope`, `-u http://HOST:PORT/` holds the host to that port the same way: a link or a script's URL to another port of HOST is outside the scope, whatever `-fs` says, and the summary's `skipped` names it with the reason `outside the scope: the targets name this host with another port only`.
A URL on the scheme's default port (`-u https://HOST/`) holds the host to 80 and 443.
The summary's `counts` sort every URL row of the crawl's scope:
A request to a host outside the scope is not sent.
`-v` adds the URL, `-s` prints the inputs only, and several keywords print one block each.
With `-input-cmd` the position is shown, not the command's output.
Five unanswered requests in a row stop the run, because the target is down. The exit code is 3 and the origin is listed under "did not answer".
With `-se` the run stops after twice `-t` failures of any kind in a row, as in ffuf. `-se-after N` names that number.
`-sf`, `-sa` and `-maxtime-job` say what they did in the summary. The first two end with exit 4, the last adds a note.
A report that cannot be written is a `failed` entry, not a silent loss. The exit code is 3. The place is tested before the first request.
Calibration that could filter nothing is exit 3, not 0
A name ending `.csv`, `.ecsv`, `.html`, `.md` or `.ejson` takes that format without `-of`.
`-x` sends every request through an http, https, socks5 or socks5h proxy.
**Reports**: `-o FILE` with `-of json|ejson|csv|ecsv|html|md|all`, `-od DIR` and `-or`.
Without a source, azhaq looks in all four and says so when the name is in two with different values.
A value read from an answer can never change the scheme, host or port of a request. ffuf's `-preflight-anyhost` does not exist here.
A `Host: TOKEN` line or a `TOKEN/path` is refused: `preflight/postflight failed … cannot choose where requests go`. The failure makes exit 3.
`… is outside the scope` means the file names a host the run may not touch: `-allow HOST` adds it, next to the host of `-u`, which `-allow` no longer adds for you.
With `-preflight` or `-postflight` the inputs run one at a time, whatever `-t` says: each input's preflight, request and postflight are one sequence, and the next starts when it ends.
A note in the summary says so.
Without it a note says nothing was calibrated.
`-rate` paces its guesses like any request, and `-max-requests` counts them.
ffuf's are unpaced and not counted.
column4: note:describes ffuf's own calibration, not azhaq's

column3: ffuf's calibration filters one exact size, word count or line count that all its answers share. When the page changes on every request (a nonce, a counter, a build stamp) they share none, and ffuf lists every word, a virtual host or a path alike.
column4: test:cmd/azhaq:TestFuzzAutoCalibrationHoldsAPageThatChangesEachTime;note:describes ffuf's own calibration, which azhaq repeats with -ac off

column3: `fuzz` then reads what the page is from the answers of one status: the title they all have, the tag names they use and the words they all show. A match of that status with the same title, only those tags and at least 80% of those words is held back, and the summary counts them: `7 answers looked like the page that names that cannot exist get … and were held back, not listed (-ac=false lists them)`. A host or path that answers a page of its own is listed.

The page needs a title all answers share or at least 3 shared words. Without them calibration filters nothing: the summary says `auto-calibration: … set no filter and the wildcard answers are listed with the matches` and the exit is 3, because the list may hold wildcard answers.
With `-ac` on, answers are read into memory until calibration is done (and for the whole run with `-ach`, or when a page shape was learned), where ffuf only counts them.
An empty line of a wordlist is a word:
`azhaq resume -db FILE` asks only the others, so no input goes out twice, and its summary counts only what it newly did. Workers answer out of order, so the inputs asked are not always the first N.
`-quiet` prints no matches and no progress, only the summary; the matches are still counted and kept by `-db` and `-o`.
The command is stored without its secrets (`-b`, a credential `-H`, a proxy's password), with its files by full path:

With `-db`, the workspace holds the command from the first request on, and the inputs asked and the matches so far are kept every second. A run killed with SIGKILL, a crash or a power cut is continued by `azhaq resume -db FILE` from the last second kept: the inputs it asked since then are asked again (the summary counts them), and a write (`-X POST`, `-d`) the ledger lists is never sent again, whatever it was for. A run with `-recursion` or `-control` goes on from its first input, since the directories found and the filters changed are not in what is kept; it too holds back the writes already sent. With `-ledger off` nothing says what was sent after the last second, so a write may go out twice.
The `-start N` in the summary's command is the first input not asked in a row. Run by hand, it may repeat inputs past it; `azhaq resume` does not.
With `-allow 10.0.0.5`, a word that names another host is counted and not sent.
A `Host` from a `-request` file is not typed by you. One that differs from `-u` is refused unless `-allow` names it.
A request to a host outside the scope is not sent, and the summary counts it.
Every request goes through the run's budget and pace (`-max-requests`, `-rate`) and the ledger, and stops at the kill file.
Without it, `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` apply by Go's rule, as in ffuf: a loopback target stays direct: [Proxies](../CONCEPTS.md#proxies). `-replay-proxy` is not read from the environment.
They are not requests to the target, so they are not in the ledger, the budget or the pace.
Send text from a pipe or a file to Slack, Discord, Telegram, Teams, Google Chat, Pushover, Gotify, SMTP or any URL.
Prints each message as it was sent, and a summary that names every entry a message did not reach.
The summary on stderr names every provider entry that a message did not reach.
A delivery that did not arrive is named in the summary, and the exit code is 3. Where notify prints a line and exits 0, `azhaq notify` and `azhaq watch` do not exit 0 over a lost message.
Exit 2 and nothing sent when:
- the config has a key the schema does not have
- `-p` or `-id` is a filter that matches nothing
Without a config, `azhaq notify` and `watch -notify-config` stop with exit 2 and send nothing.
A key the schema does not have is an error (exit 2). A mistyped `slack_webhok_url` is not a silent hole.
`-no-color` and `-disable-update-check` are accepted and do nothing.
Without `-bulk`, a line is a message. With `-bulk`, a message holds as many lines as fit in `-cl` characters (default 4000).
`-rl` (default 1) is the most requests a second, for every provider. 0 means no limit.
Each message goes to every entry of every provider, in this order:
Discord: 2,000 characters to an embed, at most three embeds to a post, more posts for more text.
STARTTLS is used when the server offers it and `smtp_disable_starttls` is not set.
An answer of 300 or more is a failure.
notify does not look.
column4: note:says what the notify tool does, not azhaq

column3: These rules hold for every message azhaq sends, `azhaq watch`'s included.
Every request has 30 seconds.

A 429, a 5xx or a failed connection is tried again, up to three times. The wait is `Retry-After` (seconds or a date, up to a minute) or 1 and 2 seconds. A longer `Retry-After` is reported, not waited out.
Any other 4xx is not tried again. A redirect to another host is not followed.
Certificates are verified, also through `-proxy`.
azhaq checks for no updates.
A message longer than a service takes is sent in parts, not cut.

With `-ledger FILE`, every request is a line of that [ledger](../OUTPUT.md#the-ledger): class `source`, a try of a delivery each, the webhook by its scheme and host only. An SMTP delivery is one `tcp` line to the mail server. Without `-ledger` nothing is kept: `notify` has no workspace to keep a ledger beside. `azhaq watch` records its notifications in its workspace's ledger
Failures are never silent. The summary lists each provider and the ids of its entries that did not get a message, with the reason.
A webhook URL is a secret. azhaq never prints it, and the ledger lists it by its host.
The host is not hidden: it is what names the hook that failed, and the lookup of it is on the network anyway.
Keep the secret in the path, the query or the user part of the URL, or in the provider config, not in the host name.
column4: note:advice on where to put a secret

column3: No error holds a URL's path or query, or a token, key, password or header value of the config, even if the server repeats it.
`watch` keeps URLs off the command line too, where `ps` shows them to every user: `-notify @FILE` and `AZHAQ_NOTIFY`
`counts` has `delivered`, `requests sent` (every try of every delivery, the number of lines `-ledger` lists) and, when any message needed more tries, `retried`.
Marks a page `partial` when it was not fully loaded, and the run exits 3.

A picture that comes out a size other than `-shot-size` asks for (not with `-shot-fullpage`, which is as tall as the page) is a failed target (`the picture came out WxH, not the WxH -shot-size asked for`), not a silently smaller picture.
`-nmap` takes every open TCP port of the file, as `gowitness scan nmap` does, because nmap names a web port by guesses (Juice Shop on 3001 is `nessus`).
A port that nmap named a web service is tried over its scheme; any other over https, then http.
`-service NAMES` and `-service-contains http` take only those services, `-p` only those ports, `-skip-port` leaves ports out, and `-open-only=false` also tries ports nmap did not find open.
The summary says how many ports were tried and how many answered with a page.

A port nmap did not name a web service is tried because nmap's guess cannot be trusted, so a port that gives no page is no web service there, not a failure: a note counts such ports and the exit code stays 0, as `gowitness scan nmap` exits 0 on a scan with an ssh port.
A port nmap named http or https is an ordinary target: its failure is counted and listed like any other target's, and the exit code is the shared rule's (3 when no target answered).
A failure (a timeout, a refused connection, a name that does not resolve, a page Chrome could not take) has `failed: true` and its `error`, and the text line ends `failed: ` and the error.

An answer that is not a failure (no web service on the ports guessed for a bare name, a target outside the scope, a page left alone by `-shot-codes`) has `failed: false` and a `note`, and the text line ends `no screenshot: ` and the note.
A scan file's port that nmap did not name a web service, and gave no page, has no row:
A run that stopped before it came to a target leaves it without a row: `azhaq resume` asks it.
The summary's results are the pictures, and `without a screenshot` counts the other rows, so the rows printed are the two added.
All of it is read from events Chrome already sends. It costs no request.
A page whose own in-scope assets did not load is `partial`, and the run exits 3.
A page that is partial only because assets of hosts outside the scope were blocked is marked and noted. The run still exits 0, because the scope is yours.
A page that was not fully loaded when the picture was taken has these fields, and the run exits 3:
`unloaded`: its images, styles, scripts, fonts and media that did not load, or failed.
Chrome is held to the scope. What a page loads from a host outside it, such as a CDN's styles, fonts and scripts, is never asked for. The picture is drawn without it.
To allow them, use `-allow cdn.jsdelivr.net`. When no scope was named, add `-allow` for the page's own host too, since any `-allow` replaces the default scope.
This does not change the exit code:
Nothing outside the scope is loaded by default.
Chrome is started once for the run, and each page is taken after its load event, once nothing it shows is still on its way.

Without `-shot-wait`, a page is taken early only after its load event (its images and styles are then in) and only when nothing can still change it: no script, frame, object, embed or refresh, no CSS animation or transition still running (a fade-in), no autoplaying `<video>` or `<audio>`, and Chrome has painted it and its fonts are in. Any other page is given 1.5 s after its load event, since a timer or an animation may draw at any moment.
`-shot-wait 3s` waits 3 s for every page, scripts or not; `-shot-wait 0` takes the page at once.

`AZHAQ_CHROME` names the browser. Where the system gives Chrome no sandbox (a container, AppArmor), Chrome does not start: `shots` stops with exit 2 before any request, and the error names `-chrome-no-sandbox`. With that flag Chrome is started once more without a sandbox and the summary says so

A URL you give is shot as given, one file for each page, named like `http_host_port_path_hash.png`; with a scheme it is one target and one row (where Chrome ended is in `final_url`, also when the page redirected to another scheme or host), and only a bare name or `host:port` is tried on both schemes. The URLs a run finds itself are shot only when they are front pages.
A page that calls `alert()` on load has its dialog accepted and is shot. Nothing waits for a click.

Every download is refused and listed, and a window a page opens (`window.open`, a `_blank` link) is closed as it opens. A page's own writes are refused and mapped. Chrome saves nothing to disk but the picture.
At a set `-rate`, a page's time runs from when it last moved. A slow pace gives whole pictures, not blank ones.
When the budget was spent before the page loaded, the note says so:
Without `-db` it uses the last run's database. `-format` defaults to `jsonl`.

A format that finds nothing writes nothing and says why on stderr; `openapi` writes a description with no paths instead (below), and `findings`/`findings-md` write an explicit empty record set. The exit code is 0, except for `graphql` and `sdl`: when no GraphQL schema was read they write nothing, fail with `no GraphQL schema in DB: map with -graphql …` and exit 1.
Screenshots are embedded, 560 pixels wide. The page opens from any directory.
A picture file missing from where the run named it and from beside the database is listed as not found.
The address a description was read from (`/openapi.json`) is not a path of the API it describes: it is left out unless the description lists it.

A workspace with no API route gives one too, such as a run whose target did not answer. Its `paths` is `{}`, stderr says `azhaq export: no API routes found on ORIGIN: wrote a description with no paths`, and the exit code is 0.
Every `operationId` is unique. A served description's keep theirs. A repeat gets `_2`, `_3` in path order: `/blog` and `/blog/` are both `get_blog`.
Templates that differ only by their parameter names are one path: the served description's, else the first.
Every `{name}` in a path is a declared path parameter, and a parameter is listed once.
Component names that OpenAPI does not allow are renamed, with their references.
A route the run did not request (`skipped`, kept out by `-deny-path`) has no GET or HEAD of azhaq's making in it. A tool importing the description would send one.
`-safe` leaves those operations out, for a tool that must not touch them.
